nodes.label: Strategy
nodes.question: What is the significance of the assessments approved during IPBES-11?
nodes.answer: Both assessments stress urgency and are policy-ready for governments to implement globally.
nodes.paragraph: Abstract The eleventh session of the Intergovernmental Science-Policy Platform on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services (IPBES-11) was held in Windhoek, Namibia, in December 2024. Approval of two assessments were the highlights of this plenary: the thematic assessment of the interlinkages among biodiversity, water, food and health - the so-called Nexus Assessment, and the thematic assessment of the underlying causes of biodiversity loss, determinants of transformative change and options for achieving the 2050 vision for bio - diversity the so-called Transformative Change Assessment. Yet the negotiations on the summaries for policymakers for those two assessments were marked more by national interests than by science. The authors were frequently challenged to justify evidence ex - pressed in plain English, and the three years of work with its original scientific language was weakened by bureaucratically-driven wordsmithing. The assessments were finally approved with a range of response options and ways forward. Both assessments stress urgency and are policy-ready to be taken up by governments for implementation globally. IPBES continues ringing the scientific alarm bell, and science hopes that bell is heard. Keywords Science-policy Nexus assessment Transformative change Stakeholders Nature conservation Sustainable futures 1 3 Biodiversity and Conservation (2025) 34:715 721 Introduction In December 2024, the eleventh session of the Intergovernmental Science-Policy Platform on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services (IPBES-11) was hosted by the Namibian Govern - ment, marking the first IPBES plenary on African ground, fittingly with David Obura from Kenya in the Chair.

nodes.label: Management
nodes.question: What challenge does IPBES face despite receiving pledges from member states?
nodes.answer: The overall budgetary situation of IPBES remains constrained with little room for growth.
nodes.paragraph: More than 800 participants from more than 120 member states were registered, with some attending through online teleconferencing. Executive Secretary Anne Larigauderie announced her impending retirement subsequently recognised in the final session with well-deserved thanks for her efforts in steering IPBES during its growth phase. She also announced four more member states have joined IPBES; viz. Kazakhstan, Lesotho, Seychelles, and Somalia, bringing the total to 147 member states, or 75% of the nations of the world. Activities of IPBES reported by the Executive Secretary underline the continuous high level of knowledge generation and management, as well as in capacity building, other knowledge systems, policy support, and more. The breadth of these activities was recog - nized in 2024 through IPBES being a joint winner of the Blue Planet Prize, awarded to individuals or organizations that have made significant contribution to improving the global environment. The prize had an award of U$ 500.0, an amount being incorporated into the IPBES budget. Despite that boost, and significant pledges by some member states, the overall budgetary situation of IPBES remains constrained, with little room for growth.

nodes.question: What does the IMF suggest emerging markets and developing economies should prioritize concerning AI?
nodes.answer: The IMF suggests that emerging markets and developing economies should prioritize developing digital infrastructure and digital skills to participate effectively in AI development.

Top. https://doi.org/10.1140/epjs/s11734-25-1561-8THEEUROPEAN PHYSICAL JOURNAL SPECIAL TOPICS Regular Article The impact of arti cial intelligence: from cognitive costs to global inequality Guy Pai c1, ,aand Leonid Serkin2,b 1Instituto de Ciencias Nucleares, Universidad Nacional Aut onoma de M exico, Apartado Postal 70-543, 4510 Ciudad de M exico, Mexico 2Facultad de Ciencias, Universidad Nacional Aut onoma de M exico, Circuito Exterior s/n, Ciudad Universitaria, Coyoac an, 4510 Ciudad de M exico, Mexico Received 5 November 2024 / Accepted 3 March 2025 The Author(s) 2025 Abstract In this paper, we examine the wide-ranging impact of arti cial intelligence on society, focusing on its potential to both help and harm global equity, cognitive abilities, and economic stability. We argue that while arti cial intelligence o ers signi cant opportunities for progress in areas like healthcare, edu-cation, and scienti C research, its rapid growth mainly driven by private companies may worsen global inequalities, increase dependence on automated systems for cognitive tasks, and disrupt established eco- nomic paradigms.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Governance|Partnerships for the goals|Global financial governance|Global monetary policies_qna_003
nodes.label: Analysis
nodes.question: What does the International Monetary Fund (IMF) say about the energy demands of AI development?
nodes.answer: The IMF states that the computational power required to sustain AI development is rapidly growing and could consume as much energy as entire countries in the near future, raising concerns about smaller countries' ability to participate in AI development.
nodes.paragraph: We emphasize the critical need for strong governance and ethical guidelines to tacklethese issues, urging the academic community to actively participate in creating policies that ensure the bene its of arti cial intelligence are shared fairly and its risks are managed e ectively. 1 Introduction Arti cial intelligence1(Al) is transforming the way we live. The impact of AI represents a rapid and transformative shift in society, comparable only to some of the most remarkable milestones in human history, such as the discovery of re, the Industrial Revolution, or the invention of the automobile. Today, society is facing the rapid rise of I,which like a massive tsunami is permeating every aspect of life. From sophisticated reinforcement learning algorithms that master chess and other games [ 2] to Al-driven coding assistants [ 3] and large language models (LLMs) like ChatGPT (4) or DeepSeek [ 5], these innovations not only empower individuals to learn and innovate but also help build a more inclusive, interconnected global community. However, every technological leap brings not only opportunities but also risks and unforeseen consequences.

nodes.label: Methodology
nodes.question: What method is used to extract factors from the macroeconomic variables in the study?
nodes.answer: The study uses 2SKF, an unsupervised factor extraction procedure, to extract factors from a large set of Spanish macroeconomic variables.
nodes.paragraph: In this paper, we analyse the short-run relationship between economic activity and CO 2emissions in Spain, by tting a SADFM to annual rates of growth of Spanish CO 2 emissions with the factors extracted by 2SKF from a large set of Spanish macroeco-nomic variables. 2SKF is an unsupervised factor extraction procedure, which combinesinformation contained in all macroeconomic variables independently from the target variable. Additionally, we also consider factor extraction orientated towards pre- diction of the rate of growth of CO 2emissions. In particular, we extract factors using partial least squares (PLS) as proposed by Wold ( 1966 ). We conclude that the explana- tory power of selected economic variables is larger than that of common economic factors when the latter are extracted using the 2SKF procedure. However, the pre-dictive power of the common factors increases when they are extracted using PLS. We nd that the PLS common factors recover some explanatory power for explaining CO 2emissions beyond the information content of the selected individual economic indicators. Our results somehow differ from those found by Bennedsen et al. ( 2021 ) for the US economy as the outstanding predictors for CO 2emissions in Spain are private consumption and maritime transport of merchandise, while theirs rely more on IP .
